feed.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT

entry.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT
entry.summary:
Ensuring the safety of cryptographic signature schemes requires a careful balance between complexity and practical security. Introducing additional commitment to a subset of the script within each signature may increase complexity, but this step can be justified if it provides tangible security benefits, such as protecting users from fund loss. Rejecting added complexity purely for simplicity’s sake is not advisable when it compromises safety.
Relying on the notion that an approach seems unbreakable simply because no explicit vulnerability is detected is discouraged in cryptography. This mindset represents an anti-pattern, where subjective confidence replaces rigorous analysis. Without concrete evidence that more comprehensive commitment is possible or beneficial—such as committing to more information than what script masking enables—there is little incentive to pursue greater complexity. Script masking offers a practical solution for scenarios requiring flexibility, such as spending different scripts with the same signature, while also maintaining generality for use cases like Lightning Network’s eltoo protocol and complex scripting variations.
By employing script masking, systems can mitigate risks associated with key and value reuse across channels. For instance, encoding unique channel identifiers into masked scripts ensures that signatures remain bound to specific channels, even when similar keys or capacities are reused. This mechanism helps prevent accidental cross-channel spending and enhances overall robustness.
The NOINPUT primitive raises significant concerns due to its minimal contextual commitment, potentially exposing users to dangers such as unintended spends. The suggestion to label it as "_UNSAFE" reflects these apprehensions. While accepting some degree of risk may be tolerable for certain users, widespread adoption of primitives with insufficient safeguards remains contentious. Committing to masked scripts stands out as a substantive security improvement; if this technique also facilitates safer construction of advanced protocols, it further justifies its adoption.
Additional measures, such as ensuring outputs and inputs are clearly defined during transactions, can provide reassurance even in transactions viewed as inherently risky. By directing payments back to oneself, one can mitigate the perceived dangers associated with constructs like NOINPUT, though such arrangements should not substitute for thorough protocol design.
For further technical details on script masking, refer to [this resource](https://lists.linuxfoundation.org/pipermail/bitcoin-dev/2018-December/016539.html).
